t: Find the Value of the Partition — Minimum Adjacent Difference After Sorting
o: We split nums into two non-empty groups minimizing |max(nums1) − min(nums2)|. After sorting, the optimal partition always separates two ADJACENT elements: max(nums1) and min(nums2) are just some element a and the smallest element of the other group, and the best possible pairing is a consecutive pair in sorted order. Example 1 sorted is [1,2,3,4]; splitting between 2 and 3 gives value 1. Example 2 sorted is [1,10,100]; the best adjacent gap is 10−1=9.
k: Sort, then the answer is the minimum difference between consecutive elements.

a.i: In sorted order, choosing max(nums1)=x and min(nums2)=y with x<y is achievable iff everything ≤x goes left and everything ≥y goes right; the cost is y−x. Minimizing over all splits equals minimizing adjacent differences.
s: Scan consecutive pairs, tracking the minimum difference.

w: Trivially short once the adjacency insight lands. Common pitfall: trying to enumerate partitions exponentially. Follow-up: maximize the value instead (answer becomes max−min of extremes split).
